question: Which explanation of this one case survives the evidence?

collier2011.cite: Collier (2011). Understanding Process Tracing. PS: Political Science & Politics, October 2011: 823 ff.
collier2011.checked: every quote read word for word in the text copy of the published PDF in the user's research library (No. 284) on 20 Nov 2026; pages are the journal's (823–827 used); the volume, issue and last page were not on the pages read; words split by line-end hyphens are rejoined

steps.title: Pose rival hypotheses
steps.text: Write down every explanation that could have produced the outcome, each as a chain of steps, before looking for evidence.

quotes.text: the systematic examination of diagnostic evidence selected and analyzed in light of research questions and hypotheses posed by the investigator.
Careful, analytically informed specification of hypotheses is essential both in selecting and interpreting pieces of evidence, and in weighing them against one another.

steps.title: Describe each step
steps.text: Establish what happened at each moment of the sequence. A chain can only be traced if each link is well described.

quotes.text: the descriptive component of process tracing begins not with observing change or sequence, but rather with taking good snapshots at a series of specific moments.

steps.title: Hoop tests
steps.text: Look for evidence a hypothesis cannot do without. If it is missing, the hypothesis is out; if present, it merely stays in the running.

quotes.text: Hoop tests do not confirm a hypothesis, but they can eliminate it.

steps.title: Smoking-gun tests
steps.text: Look for evidence that only one hypothesis would produce. Finding it strongly supports that hypothesis; not finding it clears nobody.

quotes.text: this provides a sufficient but not necessary criterion for accepting the causal inference. It can strongly support a given hypothesis, but failure to pass does not reject it.

steps.title: Combine and eliminate
steps.text: Single decisive tests are rare. Combine several: rule rivals out with hoop tests and back the survivor with the rest.

quotes.text: single tests that accomplish this are rare in social science, but this leverage may be achieved by combining multiple tests, which together support one explanation and eliminate all others.

exercise.title: Who killed John Straker?
exercise.intro: Collier teaches process tracing with the Sherlock Holmes story “Silver Blaze”. The trainer John Straker is found dead. Three suspects: the visitor Simpson, Straker himself, and the racehorse. Reveal the clues in any order and watch which suspects survive.

quote.text: when the investigator has eliminated all plausible alternatives, the remaining scenario must be the correct one.

exercise.data_label: The clues and how each is classified are Collier's (2011, tables 4–6), from a work of fiction.
exercise.weights_note: The bar lengths are only illustrative: a straw in the wind multiplies a suspect's weight by 1.5, a passed hoop test by 1.2, a smoking gun by 4, and a failed hoop test removes the suspect. Collier gives no numbers.

clues.label: Simpson's weapon
clues.says: Simpson carried a potential murder weapon. He passes this hoop test, so he stays a suspect, but it proves nothing (table 4).

clues.label: Curried mutton
clues.says: The opium that drugged the stable boy was hidden in curry that only someone in Straker's household could have added. Simpson fails this hoop test and is eliminated (table 6).

clues.label: Savage blow
clues.says: Straker's head was shattered by a heavy blow he could not have dealt himself. He fails this hoop test and is eliminated (table 6).

clues.label: Bill in his pocket
clues.says: A bill for an expensive dress his wife knew nothing about suggests money trouble and a motive to fix the race: a straw in the wind (tables 3 and 6).

clues.label: Surgical knife
clues.says: An unusual surgical knife was found with Straker. Read as exceptionally unusual it is a smoking gun for a plan to harm the horse; read as only somewhat unusual, a straw in the wind (table 5).

clues.label: Matches and candle
clues.says: Matches and a candle, and a horse gone at night, fit an attempt on the horse that frightened it into a fatal kick: a straw in the wind (table 6).

clues.label: Form of death
clues.says: So unusual a death points to an unusual cause, the horse's kick: a straw in the wind (table 6).

limits: The exercise's bar lengths are not from Collier, who classifies the tests but gives no numbers; they only show the direction of each test.
Van Evera's (1997) and Bennett's (2010) original formulations of the tests, on which Collier builds, were not read.
The step texts in our own words are summaries of the quotes beside them; the quotes are the authority.
